- If sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is consistently negative (≤0.33), model often underestimates; adjust downward bias or add small upward correction.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >+5% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots; apply a “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast by 1–2% per day post-spike.
- When true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 80), model often fails to recognize it; add a “reversion buffer” to forecast, especially if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- If model forecast is rising steadily (e.g., +0.5–1% daily) but true outcome shows downward drift, reduce forecast slope by 10–20% if sentiment is weak or mixed.
- For 30-day horizon, if sentiment is volatile or mixed (alternating 0.33–0.67), model often overfits short-term noise; use smoother trend or average of 3–5 prior days for correction.
- If true outcome is below 75 and model is above 80, apply “floor correction”: cap forecast at 78–80 if sentiment is negative or neutral.
- If sentiment is high but true outcome is low, model may be “overconfident”; reduce forecast by 1–3% per day if sentiment >0.75 and price drops >1% from prior day.
